newsitem.title: USA: NYS to collect gas, cigarette taxes on reservations.
newsitem.headline: NYS to collect gas, cigarette taxes on reservations.

text.p: New York State said on Tuesday that it took its first step to collect sales and excise taxes on gasoline and cigarettes sold to non-Native Americans who buy those products on reservations.

The state said it mailed registration packets to the Indian Nations, Indian retailers and off-reservation wholesalers, which inform them that after April 1, they will be obliged to collect these taxes.
About 3,000 convenience stores throughout New York State sued to force the state to collect the taxes, saying the reservations' tax-free status gave them an unfair advantage.

A state judge in mid-September ordered New York State to start collecting the taxes within 120 days, but the Pataki Administration appealed the decision, saying it was too broad and the issue should be solved through talks with Native Americans. But if agreement were not reached by the deadline, Gov George Pataki had said the taxes would be collected.

Initial estimates showed that the state could get about $110 million of annual revenues from the taxes. The issue was quite controversial, however, as court sources, who declined to be named, have said the Pataki Administration feared Native Americans might launch strong, perhaps violent protests.

Under the state's new plan, its tax department will calculate how much tax-free cigarettes, motor and diesel fuel a reservation can get, based on the "probable demand" from the Native American Nation's members. Coupons for buying tax-free products will then be distributed to registered dealers.

Saying Pataki respected the sovereignty of the Native American Nations and stll wanted a negotiated resolution, state Taxation and Finance Commissioner Michael Urbach, in prepared remarks, said: "In the absence of a tax compact, or any good faith efforts by the First Nations Business League to reach mutual agreement, the state has been forced to proceed with the implementation of tax regulations." He added that the state's talks with the Haudenosaunee tribe likely would produce a settllement and urged other tribes to follow suit.
